mcqs.question: In the used-set permutation generator, why is `result.append(path[:])` used instead of `result.append(path)`?
options: Without the copy, result would store references to the same list, which later pops would mutate into an incorrect final state
path[:] runs faster because it avoids a function call
append() requires an immutable argument in Python
It converts the list into a tuple for hashing
mcqs.explanation: path is one mutable list reused across the whole search; appending it directly stores a reference, and every subsequent pop() (the unexplore step) would then be visible through that same reference, so every recorded 'solution' ends up looking like the final, emptied path. path[:] makes an independent snapshot at that moment. append() has no immutability requirement, and no tuple conversion is happening here.

mcqs.question: What is the main advantage of the in-place swap approach to generating permutations over the used-set approach?
options: It produces permutations in a more intuitive, easier-to-trace order
It handles duplicate elements more simply than the used-set version
It has a better time complexity than the used-set version
It avoids O(n) extra space for tracking used elements, at the cost of mutating the input array
mcqs.explanation: Swapping elements into position reuses the input array itself instead of allocating a separate used array or set, trading that O(n) space for temporarily mutating (and later restoring) the caller's array. Both approaches are the same time complexity, the swap version's output order is actually less intuitive to trace, and duplicate-handling is trickier with swapping, not simpler.

mcqs.question: Generating permutations of [1,1,2], you sort the input and skip a candidate equal to the previous one at the same depth if the previous one hasn't been used yet. What does this correctly prevent?
options: The same numeric value from ever appearing at more than one position across all outputs
The recursion from exceeding its maximum depth
Any permutation from containing the value 1 more than once
Re-deriving the same permutation multiple times by choosing between two indistinguishable duplicate values at the same position
mcqs.explanation: Two equal values at the same tree depth are indistinguishable — choosing 'the first 1' vs 'the second 1' for this position produces the same resulting permutation, so skipping the repeat avoids counting it twice. The same value legitimately does appear at different positions in different valid permutations (1,1,2 and 1,2,1 are both valid), and this check has nothing to do with recursion depth limits.

mcqs.question: Instead of the same-level check, a duplicate-handling implementation skips any element equal to one already present anywhere in the current path. For [1,1,2], what happens?
options: It correctly produces exactly the 3 distinct permutations
It over-prunes and fails to produce valid permutations like 1,2,1 that legitimately reuse the value 1 at a different position
It produces duplicate permutations instead of unique ones
It throws an error because the same value appears twice in the input
mcqs.explanation: Checking against the whole path blocks placing a second, still-available copy of 1 just because a 1 already appears earlier in the path — but 1,2,1 is a genuinely distinct, valid permutation that needs a 1 placed at position 2. The correct check is narrower: same-value-at-the-same-depth-in-the-current-loop, not same-value-anywhere-in-the-path.

mcqs.question: Why does generating all permutations become impractical well before n reaches 20, even with a well-optimized implementation?
options: Because the algorithm's implementation constant is unusually large
Because most languages cap recursion depth well below 20
Because n! is the actual number of outputs, and 20! alone vastly exceeds what any system could enumerate — no implementation speedup changes the output count
Because sorting the input becomes the bottleneck at that size
mcqs.explanation: The work is at minimum proportional to the number of outputs, and 20! is roughly 2.4 x 10^18 — no amount of code optimization changes how many permutations exist to produce. Recursion depth here is only O(n), not the limiting factor, and there's no sorting step required at all in the plain generation algorithm.

mcqs.question: Asked to find the k-th lexicographic permutation of n elements, a candidate generates and sorts all n! permutations, then indexes into position k. What's the issue with this approach?
options: There is a direct O(n)-to-O(n^2) combinatorial construction that avoids generating all n! permutations entirely
It is correct and is the intended, optimal solution
It works for even n but not odd n
Sorting the permutations changes their meaning
mcqs.explanation: Fixing the first element leaves (n-1)! contiguous, equally-sized lexicographic blocks for the rest, which lets you peel off the correct element one position at a time using k // (n-1)! and k % (n-1)! — no generation or sorting needed. The brute-force approach is correct but wildly suboptimal, and the issue has nothing to do with the parity of n.
